parts.text:
25 A telescope detects and analyses some electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 2 cm.
Which type of telescope is it?
A
microwave telescope
B
optical telescope
C
radio telescope
D
X-ray telescope

hints: Convert the given wavelength to metres: $2\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ and ask which EM region contains centimetre-scale waves.
Recall the order of the EM spectrum by wavelength: X-ray is very short, optical is nanometres, microwave is millimetres to centimetres, radio is longer.
Compare $2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ with the microwave band of roughly $10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to $10^{-1}\text{ m}$ and with the much shorter optical and X-ray bands.
walkthrough: Identify the given information: the telescope detects electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $2\text{ cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$.

Recall the approximate wavelength ranges: X-rays $\sim 10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8}\text{ m}$, visible light $\sim 4 \times 10^{-7}$ to $7 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$, microwaves $\sim 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ to $3 \times 10^{-1}\text{ m}$, radio waves longer than this.
Compare $2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ with these ranges: it is much larger than X-ray and optical wavelengths but shorter than typical long radio waves.
It falls squarely inside the microwave band where wavelengths are measured in millimetres and centimetres.
Therefore the instrument that detects and analyses it is a microwave telescope. This is option A

A.explanation: A wavelength of $2\text{ cm}$ lies in the microwave region of about $1\text{ mm}$ to $30\text{ cm}$, so a microwave telescope is used.

B.explanation: Optical telescopes detect visible light of wavelength about $400$ to $700\text{ nm}$, which is far shorter than $2\text{ cm}$.

C.explanation: Radio waves have longer wavelengths, typically greater than about $10\text{ cm}$, so $2\text{ cm}$ is classified as microwave rather than radio.

D.explanation: X-rays have very short wavelengths of about $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8}\text{ m}$, many orders of magnitude smaller than $2\text{ cm}$.
